newsitem.title: USA: Jobless claims fall to lowest level in nearly year.
newsitem.headline: Jobless claims fall to lowest level in nearly year.

text.p: The number of Americans claiming first-time jobless benefits dropped last week to the lowest level in nearly a year, the government reported Thursday in the latest sign of a strong jobs market.
Weekly jobless claims fell to 299,000 in the week ended July 19 from a revised 341,000 the week before. That was far below the 333,000-level that economists had forecast.
The drop pushed weekly claims to their lowest level since the week ended July 27, 1996, when they hit 297,000.
The four-week moving average, which helps to smooth out week-to-week swings in the data, also fell. The average of claims stood at 340,750 last week, down from 349,000 the week before.
The number of people continuing to claim benefits rose slightly, to 2,302,000, in the week ended July 12, the latest week for which the data were available.
The department said 16 states and Puerto Rico reported increases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended July 12, the latest period for which those data were available.
Among the largest states were Tennessee, with 14,020 additional claims, North Carolina, with 11,734, Alabama, with 9,234, Michigan, with 7,928, and South Carolina, with 7,527.
Tennessee said it had layoffs in a wide variety of industries, while North Carolina reported layoffs in the textile, apparel, furniture, lumber and non-electrical machinery industries.

Alabama said it had layoffs in the textile, apparel, lumber and service industries. Michigan linked its rise in claims to the automobile industry, which has been laying off workers in recent weeks to retool plants for new car models.
There were seven states reporting decreases in initial claims exceeding 1,000, unadjusted, in the July 12 week.
They were New York, with 17,096 fewer filings, Ohio, with 3,376, Arkansas, with 2,890, Wisconsin, with 2,800, Texas, with 2,039, New Jersey, with 1,323, and Iowa, with 1,309.

Wisconsin reported fewer layoffs in the service industry and in manufacturing, while New Jersey said it had fewer layoffs in the transportation and service industries. The other states had no comment.
